definitions.definition: The cause of the world's origin, sustenance and dissolution, known from scripture, the purport of all the Upaniṣads.
The one non-dual reality, existence–consciousness–bliss, identical with the inner self; nirguṇa in itself, saguṇa (Īśvara) through māyā.
The nature of Brahman indicated by three words, each excluding its opposite; also the three aspects 'is, shines, dear' present in every object, as distinct from name and form.

name: Incidental and essential definitions of Brahman

definitions.definition: Brahman is defined incidentally (taṭastha) as the world-cause and essentially (svarūpa) as existence–consciousness–infinitude/bliss.

Brahman in itself is without attributes; the same Brahman with the adjunct of māyā is the Lord with attributes, object of worship, real at the empirical level. Texts teaching form serve meditation (BS 3.2.15).

Brahman associated with (or reflected in) māyā: omniscient, omnipotent creator and ruler, giver of fruits of action, object of devotion; his lordship depends on adjuncts and is real at the empirical level.
The prototype (bimba) consciousness whose reflection is the jīva.

relations.note: One entity viewed cosmically (māyā) and individually (avidyā) in the Vivaraṇa/Saṃkṣepaśārīraka usage; distinguished by Vidyāraṇya.

definitions.definition: The Lord's beginningless indescribable power of three guṇas, inferred from its effects, by which Brahman appears as the world; neither being nor non-being; removable by knowledge.

relations.note: in the later view avidyā is the material cause of superimposition

definitions.definition: For Śaṅkara, the superimposition of self and not-self, removed by discrimination; for later Advaita a positive, beginningless, indescribable power with veiling and projecting powers, the cause of saṃsāra, removed by knowledge alone.
One ignorance located in and directed to pure consciousness.
Ignorances located in the jīvas, directed to Brahman.
Ignorance is a positive though indescribable entity, known by perception ('I am ignorant'), inference and presumption.

name: The two powers of ignorance: veiling and projecting

definitions.definition: Ignorance veils the self (āvaraṇa, tamas) and projects the world and the bodies (vikṣepa, rajas).

relations.note: Śaṅkara: 'the learned call this superimposition avidyā'

definitions.definition: The appearance, like memory, of something previously seen in something else; the mutual superimposition of self and not-self, natural and beginningless, called avidyā, the root of all empirical dealings.

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's real transformation of prakṛti; Advaita accepts pariṇāma only for māyā
vivarta speaks of appearance; ajāti denies any origination at the highest level

definitions.definition: The world is an apparent, not a real, transformation of Brahman, as the snake of the rope; effects are non-different from the cause, mere names (BS 2.1.14).

Ultimate (pāramārthika: Brahman, never sublated), empirical (vyāvahārika: the waking world, sublated only by Brahman-knowledge) and apparent (prātibhāsika: dream, rope-snake, sublated by waking cognition).

The world is false (mithyā): not unreal like a hare's horn, not real like Brahman, but indescribable and sublatable; defended by the inference 'because it is seen, insentient, limited' and by five definitions.
A cognition is sublated when a later valid cognition shows its object was never as it appeared; degrees of sublatability define the levels of reality.
The inner self of every being is Brahman; difference is due only to adjuncts produced by ignorance (Kāśakṛtsna's view, accepted by Śaṅkara).

The individual self is consciousness conditioned by the inner organ (and ignorance): agent, enjoyer and transmigrant through adjuncts, in truth Brahman; explained by limitation, reflection or semblance.

name: How the one appears as many (the three theories)

definitions.definition: Three explanatory theories of the jīva and Īśvara: limitation (avaccheda, Bhāmatī), reflection (pratibimba, Vivaraṇa) and semblance (ābhāsa, Sureśvara); the tradition treats them as alternative methods (prakriyā) converging on identity.
The jīva is Brahman delimited by the inner organ, as space by a pot; nothing is added or lost.
The jīva is Brahman's reflection in avidyā/the inner organ, real and identical with the prototype; Īśvara is the prototype (or, for Sarvajñātman, the reflection in ignorance).
The jīva is a mere semblance of consciousness in the intellect, neither real nor the original; knowing it as semblance, only consciousness remains (Sureśvara; cf. BS 2.3.50).
The absolute (pāramārthika) jīva, in truth Brahman; the empirical (vyāvahārika) jīva, the reflection in the intellect; the illusory (prātibhāsika) jīva of dream.
There is one jīva whose ignorance projects all others, as in dream; associated with dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda (Prakāśānanda; surveyed by Madhusūdana).
Jīvas are many, each with its own ignorance; one is liberated while others remain bound.
Dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi: the world exists only while perceived, like dream (Prakāśānanda); sṛṣṭi-dṛṣṭi: Īśvara creates an empirical world that exists before and apart from individual perception (majority view).
From the highest standpoint nothing is ever born — not from itself, another, both or neither; creation-teachings are means to lead the mind (GK 3.15).
Brahman is taught by negating every specification; negation terminates in Brahman, the 'reality of the real', which is not negated.

relations.note: the witness of the three states is the fourth

definitions.definition: The unchanging consciousness that illumines the mind's modes, the three states and ignorance itself, never an object (DDV 1; the theatre-lamp of Pañcadaśī 10).
Consciousness reveals itself without being an object of another cognition; defined by Citsukha.

relations.note: gross = food sheath; subtle = vital, mental, intellectual sheaths; causal = bliss sheath

definitions.definition: Gross (quintuplicated elements, waking), subtle (seventeen members, dream) and causal (ignorance, deep sleep) bodies; the self is none of them.
Food, vital air, mind, intellect and bliss sheaths, which seem to cover the self; taught progressively so that the self is known as distinct from each; the bliss-sheath is not Brahman (Śaṅkara).

name: The three states and the fourth (avasthā-traya, turīya)

definitions.definition: Waking (viśva), dream (taijasa) and deep sleep (prājña) come and go; the self as the fourth (turīya) pervades and transcends them, non-dual; analysis of the three states is a means to know the self.

name: The inner organ and its four functions

definitions.definition: One inner organ functioning as mind (doubt), intellect (decision), citta (memory) and ego (I-sense); the adjunct of the jīva, not the self.
The inner organ goes out through the sense, takes the object's form, and the consciousness delimited by knower, mode and object become one (Vedāntaparibhāṣā ch.1).
Six means, valid for the empirical and following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā; all within the sphere of ignorance; scripture alone reveals Brahman; perception grasps being, not difference.

name: Error as appearance of the indescribable (anirvacanīya-khyāti)

definitions.definition: In error an indescribable object (neither real nor unreal) is produced by ignorance for the duration of the error; the Advaita alternative to the rival theories of error.

name: The mode in the form of the partless (akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti)

definitions.definition: The mental mode arising from the mahāvākya that destroys ignorance and then itself subsides; Brahman is pervaded by the mode but not illumined by the reflected consciousness in it.

name: Pervasion by the mode but not by its result

definitions.definition: Ordinary objects are pervaded by both the mental mode and the reflected consciousness (its 'result'); Brahman, being self-luminous, only by the mode, which removes ignorance.

Four Upaniṣadic sentences of identity — prajñānaṃ brahma, ahaṃ brahmāsmi, tat tvam asi, ayam ātmā brahma — understood through implication as conveying a partless meaning; the means of liberating knowledge.
Since 'that' (omniscient Lord) and 'thou' (limited self) conflict in their direct meanings, the contradictory elements are dropped and pure consciousness retained, as in 'this is that Devadatta'.

relations.note: both treat teachings as means relative to the student

definitions.definition: The teaching method of scripture: provisionally superimpose (creation, sheaths, attributes) and then retract, leaving the substratum; creation-teachings are means (GK 3.15).

name: The method of pointing out Arundhatī (arundhatī-nyāya)

definitions.definition: Leading from the gross to the subtle step by step, as one points to a faint star by first showing a bright neighbouring one; used for the progressive teaching of the sheaths.

Any method that brings one to know the inner self is valid, and none is fixed (Sureśvara); the ancients, intent on the oneness of the self, were indifferent to the explanation of the empirical (Appayya).
Discrimination of the eternal and non-eternal, dispassion, the six virtues, and longing for liberation — the prerequisites of the inquiry into Brahman.
Calm, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith and concentration (BS 3.4.27; BĀU 4.4.23).
The threefold discipline of the qualified seeker (BĀU 2.4.5): hearing removes doubt about the means (scripture's purport), reflection doubt about the object, contemplation contrary habitual notions.
Hearing is principal, the other two auxiliaries.
Contemplation is principal; the purified mind is the instrument.

Meditation on the qualified Brahman or a symbol, seated and one-pointed, until death, purifies and steadies the mind and leads to the Brahma-world; meditation on the attributeless leads to knowledge (Pañcadaśī 9).

Savikalpa and nirvikalpa samādhi as auxiliaries of contemplation, with eight limbs and four obstacles (Vedāntasāra); six samādhis inner and outer (Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka); the state of no-mind (GK 3.32). Samādhi is a means; knowledge liberates.

name: Knowledge, destruction of tendencies, dissolution of mind

definitions.definition: Vidyāraṇya's triad, practised together for the stable freedom of the jīvanmukta.

relations.note: purified by duties the student acquires the four means

definitions.definition: Works cannot remove ignorance, being not opposed to it; performed without desire they purify the mind and generate the desire to know (or knowledge); knowledge excludes the sense of agency, so works and knowledge are not combined.

name: Classes of action for the seeker

definitions.definition: Desire-prompted (kāmya) and forbidden (niṣiddha) acts to be avoided; daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika) and expiatory (prāyaścitta) rites and meditations (upāsana) to be performed for purity.

Devotion to the Lord purifies and steadies the mind and is supreme among the means; defined as dwelling on one's own nature (VC 31); the knower is the highest devotee (Gītā 7.17); for Madhusūdana a rasa and supreme goal in itself.
Renunciation of works is enjoined for the knower and for the seeker (vidvat- and vividiṣā-sannyāsa); the paramahaṃsa ideal; institutionalized in the Daśanāmī order.
On knowledge, past karma is destroyed and future karma does not cling, but the body continues till prārabdha is exhausted; the knower is free while living.
At the fall of the body the knower's prāṇas do not depart; he merges, nothing new being attained.
Meditators on the qualified Brahman go by the path of light to the Brahma-world and are liberated with its ruler at the end of the cycle.
Not produced but eternal: the bodiless nature of the self, the attainment of bliss and cessation of sorrow, revealed by knowledge; one in all (BS 3.4.52); no return.
Accumulated (burnt by knowledge), to come (does not cling) and begun (exhausted by experience, like a potter's wheel's momentum).
Protection of knowledge, austerity, absence of conflict, cessation of suffering, manifestation of bliss (Jīvanmuktiviveka ch. 4).

name: The seven states of the jīva (Pañcadaśī 7)

definitions.definition: Ignorance, veiling, projection, mediate knowledge, immediate knowledge, cessation of sorrow, unrestricted contentment.
Steady wisdom apprehending identity; virtues arising without effort; no licence for misconduct; living for others' good; unbroken realization in activity and absorption.
Those who reach the Brahma-world by meditation fulfil desires by will alone, but have no power over the world's creation and are equal to the Lord only in enjoyment (BS 4.4.8, 4.4.17, 4.4.21).
Powers belong to the realm of māyā and to saguṇa meditation; they are not liberation; the knower does not relish even the bliss of absorption (GK 3.45).
At death speech merges in mind etc.; the knower of the attributeless Brahman does not depart (his prāṇas merge here); the meditator departs by the crown channel and the path of light.
The path of the gods (beginning with light) for meditators, without return; the path of the fathers (smoke, the moon) for ritualists, with return and residual karma.

From Brahman associated with māyā arise space, air, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1) as subtle elements, then by quintuplication the gross; creation is sport, a superimposition taught to lead to the uncreated; Brahman is both material and efficient cause.
Each level of ignorance and body has a collective (cosmic) and individual aspect: Īśvara–prājña (causal), Hiraṇyagarbha–taijasa (subtle), Virāj–viśva (gross).
The gross elements are formed by combining half of each subtle element with an eighth of each of the other four.
Māyā/ignorance consists of sattva, rajas and tamas: sattva pure (adjunct of Īśvara) or impure (of jīva); tamas veils, rajas projects.
Daily (deep sleep), occasional, elemental and final (liberation).
Bliss is Brahman's nature; the bliss of deep sleep and the joys of objects are its reflections or fragments (Pañcadaśī 11–15).

Standard images used to teach non-duality: rope-snake, shell-silver, pot-space, the reflection of the sun, dream, clay and pots, the tenth man, the crystal and the red flower, the potter's wheel, the firebrand, the mirror-city, the theatre lamp, the painted canvas.
The snake seen in the rope in dim light: superimposition, the substratum, and sublation when the rope is known.
Silver seen in mother-of-pearl: error as appearance, like memory, of a previously seen thing elsewhere; the world appears real until Brahman is known.
Space enclosed in pots seems many but is one space; so the self appears as many jīvas through bodies.

name: Reflection of the sun in water

definitions.definition: The one sun appears as many trembling reflections; so Brahman appears as many jīvas sharing their adjuncts' changes.
Dream objects are real while dreaming and sublated on waking; so the waking world before knowledge; the jīva sleeps in beginningless māyā.
Pots are only clay, names being a matter of speech; so the world is non-different from Brahman (ChU 6.1.4; BS 2.1.14).
Ten men each forget to count himself; told 'you are the tenth', each knows it at once: the mahāvākya gives immediate knowledge of what was never lost.
A clear crystal appears red near a red flower; so the self appears with the qualities of its adjuncts.
The wheel keeps turning after the potter's push has ceased; so the knower's body continues until prārabdha is spent.

name: The four āmnāya maṭhas (the tradition's account)

definitions.definition: Śaṅkara founded four cardinal monasteries, each with a Veda, a mahāvākya, a first ācārya and Daśanāmī names: Śṛṅgeri (south; Yajur; ahaṃ brahmāsmi; Sureśvara; Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, Purī), Govardhana, Purī (east; Ṛg; prajñānaṃ brahma; Padmapāda; Vana, Araṇya), Śāradā, Dvārakā (west; Sāma; tat tvam asi; Hastāmalaka; Tīrtha, Āśrama), Jyotirmaṭh (north; Atharva; ayam ātmā brahma; Toṭaka; Giri, Parvata, Sāgara). The Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi pīṭha claims foundation by Śaṅkara too, which the others dispute. See lin:dasanami (U57) for the living order.

The lineage recited in the tradition: Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā (Padmabhava), Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śuka, Gauḍapāda, Govinda, Śaṅkara, and his disciples Padmapāda, Hastāmalaka, Toṭaka and the Vārttikakāra (Sureśvara).

The teacher is learned in scripture and established in Brahman, calm, compassionate, free of pride; the student approaches with humility, service and questioning, calm, self-controlled and longing for liberation; knowledge of the truth, not birth, makes the guru (Manīṣāpañcaka).
Upaniṣads, Bhagavad Gītā and Brahma Sūtras, on which every Vedānta ācārya comments.
Qualified student, subject, relation and purpose of a teaching.
Opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise, demonstration — used in hearing to determine that the Upaniṣads' purport is the non-dual Brahman (from Mīmāṃsā).
The sūtras are commented on in topic-sections, each with subject, doubt, prima facie view, conclusion and connection; commentators group and count them differently.
